title: UV Seams and Material Boundaries in Runtime Subdivision
abstract: Why a position-continuous refined mesh can still crack visually—and how geometric topology, face-varying UV topology, tangent discontinuities, and section ownership should be represented.
imageAlt: A shared geometric edge is split into UV and material-side vertices during runtime subdivision
cardImageAlt: Project material capture of the skeletal mesh wireframe before runtime subdivision
lede: A render vertex is not the same thing as a geometric vertex. Importers duplicate vertices at UV seams, hard normals, tangent discontinuities, and material boundaries. Runtime subdivision that treats those duplicates as unrelated geometry can create cracks; subdivision that welds them indiscriminately can destroy intentional discontinuities.

sections.heading: One surface carries several topologies
paragraphs: Geometric topology answers which faces share a point or edge in object space. Texture topology answers which face-corners share one UV value. Normal and tangent topology may split again at hard edges or mirrored UV charts. Material topology partitions faces into draws. These relationships overlap, but they are not identical.

A typical indexed render mesh resolves that complexity by duplicating complete vertex records. The GPU receives simple arrays, but the original equivalence information is partly lost unless the runtime system reconstructs or stores it.

rows: Material identity and sometimes UV set differ
technicalTables.caption: Welding should be decided per domain, not once for the entire packed vertex.

sections.heading: Why per-section subdivision cracks
paragraphs: Unreal submits skeletal LOD sections independently. If each material section is converted into a separate OpenSubdiv mesh, the shared material edge becomes a boundary in both refiners. Each side now applies a boundary rule using only its local neighborhood instead of the original two-sided surface neighborhood.

Even when both sides coincidentally produce the same positions, their refined normals, tangents, and UVs can differ. Animation and floating-point order can make the position mismatch visible later. The root issue is not ‘bad weights’; it is that an implementation boundary was mistaken for a geometric boundary.

sections.heading: A robust representation
paragraphs: Build one positional control mesh for the whole logical surface, or at least for each truly disconnected component. Preserve a mapping from packed render vertices to logical position vertices. Faces retain their material IDs so refined triangles can still be grouped into material draws.

Represent UVs as face-varying data: values are attached to face corners and may have a different index topology from positions. OpenSubdiv provides face-varying interpolation specifically for this case. Normal and tangent handling should be explicit—either interpolate appropriate data, evaluate limit derivatives, or recompute a tangent basis from refined geometry and face-varying UVs.

steps.title: Logical position mesh
steps.text: Weld only vertices that represent the same geometric point

steps.title: Face-varying UVs
steps.text: Keep separate values on opposite sides of a chart seam

steps.title: Derived tangents
steps.text: Evaluate or rebuild the shading frame consistently

steps.title: Section draws
steps.text: Partition refined triangles after the surface is refined

sections.heading: Material assignment after refinement
paragraphs: A child face inherits its parent face’s material ID. After uniform refinement, group the generated triangles by that ID and create section index ranges. Shared refined positions may be referenced by indices from multiple material draws; there is no requirement to duplicate position storage merely because draw calls are separate.

If the vertex factory requires interleaved attributes with one index, generate packed render vertices from tuples such as (position vertex, face-varying UV vertex, normal region, material-side requirements). This final expansion happens after logical refinement, not before it.

equations.label: Render-vertex identity
equations.expression: renderVertex = unique(positionID, uvID, normalRegion, other discontinuous attributes)
terms: Material ID usually belongs to the face/draw, but may affect which packed tuples are needed.
Two render vertices can share positionID while intentionally differing in uvID.

sections.heading: Test the boundaries, not only the center
paragraphs: Create a two-quad strip whose shared edge is a material boundary and a UV seam. Animate or deform it, refine it, and inspect both wireframe position and a checker texture. Then add a mirrored chart and a hard-normal edge. These tiny meshes expose domain mistakes more clearly than a complex character.

Use debug colors for logical position ID, UV chart, parent material, and normal region. Draw lines between packed vertices that map to the same logical position. If two material sides generate different refined geometric IDs for what should be one edge, the architecture is wrong before any shading bug is investigated.

numberedSteps.text: Mark the edge hard and verify that position stays welded while shading stays discontinuous.

numberedSteps.text: Color positionID, uvID, normal region, and parent material independently.

sections.heading: Ship criteria for discontinuities
paragraphs: The implementation is ready for broader assets only after the two-quad fixture preserves geometric continuity, keeps the UV seam discontinuous, keeps the hard-normal edge discontinuous, inherits material IDs on child faces, and remains stable under animation. A smooth character screenshot does not test those conditions independently.

references.label: Epic Games: Skeletal Mesh Rendering Paths

closing: Use one logical position topology, separate face-varying UV topology, explicit normal regions, and inherited face material IDs. Pack render vertices after refinement.
